title: Predicting Penny Stock Surges
subtitle: Can a year of price and volume data tell you a penny stock is about to run? I built the pipeline to find out — and the honest answer was "not on its own."

sections.title: The question
body: Penny stocks are famous for sudden runs. I wanted to know whether those runs leave a footprint in the weeks before they happen — in volatility, volume, or price behavior — that a simple model could learn.

I pulled a year of daily OHLCV data for 41 low-priced, high-attention tickers (plus a few steadier names like AEP for contrast), cleaned it into one pipeline, and defined a "surge window" as the 50 trading days leading up to each stock's yearly high.

sections.title: The model
body: I added rolling features (5- and 10-day moving averages, volatility, volume averages and change, daily range, close/open ratio) and trained a depth-5 decision tree with balanced class weights. The split was chronological — no shuffling — so the model never peeks at the future.

sections.title: What I took away
sections.body: Price and volume alone barely beat a coin flip at spotting surges — the model caught about 1 in 4 real surge days, and most of its surge calls were false alarms. That's a useful negative result: whatever drives these runs (news, social hype, filings) mostly isn't in the price history yet.

sections.title: What I'd do next
items: Use split-adjusted prices so reverse splits stop distorting returns and drawdowns.
Add the Reddit (r/pennystocks) and news-sentiment signals as features, timed before each surge.
Validate per ticker with walk-forward splits instead of one global cutoff.
Try models that handle imbalance better (gradient boosting, threshold tuning) and report precision-recall curves.
